summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, the closest official measure for churches and faith organisations sits inside the Other services category, NAICS 81, which includes religious organizations. In the latest BTOS period, 15.0% of firms in that category reported using AI in the last two weeks, up from 13.7% in the prior period. The survey first asked the question in September 2023, and the share reflects firms answering yes to whether they used AI in the last two weeks. No better official measure exists yet, so this page says less rather than guessing about congregational adoption specifically.

Per Gloo, AI is a foundational capability across its platform to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry and create practical value across the faith and flourishing ecosystem. Gloo AI delivers values-aligned models, developer tools, and benchmarks for faith-based organizations, with API-first support for inference, RAG, and assistant workflows. The platform is described in this page's curated points as used by thousands of US churches, and it surveys faith leaders and builds AI tooling for ministry. The material gathered here centers on sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations. No revenue or market concentration figures appear in the sources.

The sources do not report ROI percentages or cost savings for congregations. Notre Dame's Meghan Sullivan notes that many workers in the AI industry talk flippantly about job displacement and AI being able to do work faster and cheaper, but that is an observation about industry attitudes, not measured returns for faith organisations. A reader looking for hard ROI evidence will find none in these excerpts.

AI and Faith convenes ethics work and identifies emerging issues around control and power, privacy, bias and discrimination, economic well-being, and understanding what it means to be human. It notes that 85 percent of the world's population claim a religious affiliation, so these issues are deeply spiritual as well as moral. Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life, and its DELTA project centers human formation and dignity in the AI transition. Lily Abadal, a partner at Partners in Mission and faculty fellow with DELTA, says AI awareness has been evolving. No regulatory posture is specified in these sources.

Barna Group's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders, the closest thing to sector-wide survey data. Hartford Institute for Religion Research has a 45 year history of providing accurate research on churches and congregational life, and Pew Research Center periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces. A reader deciding whether to deploy should take from this that official adoption is modest and rising, faith-specific platforms exist, but measured ROI is absent and the ethical questions are treated as central rather than secondary.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, convenes a multidisciplinary community to tackle pressing ethical issues. It promotes interdisciplinary research, policy leadership, and practical models for ethical AI design, development, and deployment. The institute will host a second DELTA summit focused on human formation and dignity in the AI transition. Sullivan notes that many industry workers “talk very flippantly” about job displacement and AI’s speed and cost, while Lily Abadal observes that AI awareness is evolving.

https://www.barna.com/.brief: Barna Group presents itself as a Christian research organization offering data and insights on faith, culture, and ministry. The page advertises a free webcast replay that examines six trends affecting pastoral leadership, drawing on findings from its report *The State of Pastors, Volume 2*. It also promotes a podcast in which pastors Glenn Packiam, Rich Villodas, and Sharon Hodde Miller discuss challenges and opportunities in church leadership. Additionally, Barna reports new data on the social motivators behind why young adults attend church.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: According to Gloo, its AI offering provides models, developer tools, and benchmarks that are aligned with the values of faith-based organizations. The company describes AI as a foundational capability across its platform, intended to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry, and create practical value. Developers using Gloo AI Studio can access connected infrastructure including production environment tools, trusted content, and values-aligned models. The platform also offers API-first support for inference, RAG, and assistant workflows, with dynamic selection of the appropriate model for each request.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith is an organization that brings religious and faith-based perspectives to discussions about artificial intelligence ethics. The group argues that emerging AI issues—including control, privacy, bias, discrimination, and questions about human identity—are fundamentally moral questions, and that the world's religious traditions contain "ancient wisdom" relevant to how AI should be developed and used. The organization works to connect theologians, tech creators, researchers, and ethicists to integrate faith-based values into conversations about AI's ethical implications, aiming to introduce "humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected them both."
